field_body_text.value: DMD is a rare genetic muscle disease. It occurs primarily in males,although females can be affectedand they also pass the genetic mutation onto their children. DMD affects an estimated12,000 to15,000 people in the USand25,000 in Europe.

field_sections_json.value: [{"title":"Onset","body":"DMD is the most common childhood-onset form of muscular dystrophy. Loss of strengthand function typically first appear between3 and5 years of age."},{"title":"Cause","body":"DMD results from agenetic mutationin the DMD geneon the X chromosome. This gene regulates the production of dystrophin,aprotein essential to healthy muscle developmentand function. In people with DMD,dystrophin levelsare absent or nearly absent,which causes permanent damage to muscle cells."},{"title":"Symptoms","body":"People living with DMD experience arange of symptoms,which may include: progressive muscle weakness that worsens over time,usually beginningin the upper arms,upper legsand pelvic areaand progressing to affect the lower legs,forearms,neckand trunk; enlarged calf muscles; delays in developing motor skills such as sitting,standing or walking;; toe walkingor waddling gait;; breathing problems;; cardiomyopathy,or inflammation of the musclesin the heart;; and varying degrees of cognitive impairment affecting approximately one third of patients."},{"title":"Treatment","body":"There are no transformative therapiesand no cure for DMD. Thus,there is asignificant need for new treatment options for the disease."}]

field_body_text.value: DM1 is a rare, genetic, progressive muscle diseaseestimated to affect >40,000 people in the USand >74,000 people in Europe. The severity of symptomsand pace of progression varies.

field_sections_json.value: [{"title":"Onset","body":"Symptoms can begin at any point in an affected person’s life,depending on the DM1 subtype. Adult-onset DM1 symptoms typically appear in early teens to50 years of age."},{"title":"Cause","body":"The underlying cause of DM1 is adefective DMPK gene that encodes amutated RNA. DM1 is known as atriplet repeat disease because of the expanded number of CTG repeatsin the DMPK gene. These CTG repeats cause toxic RNA to clusterin the nucleus. The toxic RNA binds to RNA splicing proteins,causing altered splicing eventsin many other genes. This altered splicing resultsin awide range of disease symptomsand contributes to the significant disease burden."},{"title":"Symptoms","body":"People experience abroad spectrum of symptoms,including: muscle weakness throughout the body,from difficulties with facial and swallowing muscles to hand and grip weaknessto lower legand foot weakness,foot dropand resulting mobility issues;; myotonia,or difficulty relaxing musclesin the jaw,tongue,throat,lower armand hand;; respiratory issues;; gastrointestinal dysfunction throughout the GI tract;; cognitive deficits,excessive daytime sleepinessand dysregulated sleep;; and early cataracts."},{"title":"Treatment","body":"There are currently no disease-modifying treatments for DM1."}]

field_body_text.value: FSHD is a rare disease characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle,which causes profound weakness. It is estimated to affect approximately16,000 to38,000 people in the USand35,000 people in Europe.

field_sections_json.value: [{"title":"Onset","body":"There is wide variability in age of onset with FSHD. Symptoms typically begin to appear in the teen years. In some cases,individuals do not begin to experience the muscle weakness characteristic of FSHD until well into adulthood. A very rare form of FSHD,often called infantile FSHD or IFSHD,is particularly debilitating,with symptoms beginningin infancy or early childhood."},{"title":"Cause","body":"FSHD is caused by aberrant expression of agene called DUX4. In ahealthy individual,DUX4 is active for only ashort timein early embryonic development. In individuals with FSHD,the DUX4 gene remains “on” long after it is supposed to be silenced. This activation leads to surplus production of the DUX4 protein,which causes the gradual destruction of muscle cells throughout the body."},{"title":"Symptoms","body":"The symptoms of FSHD often emerge first with aloss of facial muscle strength,making it difficult to smile or use astraw. Weakness typically progresses to all major muscle groups including the arms,torso,legs,and abdomenand can lead to limited mobility. The severity of symptoms varies widely. People living with FSHD can also experience jointand spinal abnormalities,including protrusion of the shoulder blades."},{"title":"Treatment","body":"Although the genetic cause of FSHD is well understood,there are currently no approved disease-modifying treatments for FSHD."}]

He also spent several years in private practice in the litigation departments at Dechert LLP and Choate, Hall & Stewart LLP, where he represented pharmaceutical companies in complex civil litigation and investigations.

Alessandro holds a B.A. in Political Science and Italian Literature from Boston College and J.D. from Georgetown University Law Center.

","source_id":1282},{"name":"Barry Greene","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Barry has more than three decades of biopharmaceutical industry experience, including scaling innovative companies from development through commercialization across rare diseases, neuroscience, and oncology. Barry recently served as chief executive officer of Sage Therapeutics from December 2020 to July 2025, where he led the company’s focus on brain health disorders and advanced key late-stage programs, including the launch of a novel treatment for postpartum depression. Previously, he spent nearly two decades at Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, including as president and chief operating officer, helping build the company into a multi-product biopharmaceutical organization and supporting development of the first RNAi therapies. Earlier, he led global oncology strategy at Millennium Pharmaceuticals, including the approval and launch of VELCADE®.

He currently serves as lead independent director of Karyopharm Therapeutics and has served on the boards of Sage Therapeutics and Acorda Therapeutics. Mr. Greene holds a BS in industrial engineering from the University of Pittsburgh and was a Senior Scholar at Duke University’s Medical School and Fuqua School of Business.

[{"name":"Sudhir Agrawal, D.Phil.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Agrawal is a visiting professor in the Department of Medicine at the University of Massachusetts Medical School and a member of the advisory board of the Harvard Medical School Initiative for RNA Medicine. He is a founder and member of Arnay Sciences LLC. He is also a founder of Idera Pharmaceuticals, where he served in various leadership roles, including as chairman, CEO, president of research and chief scientific officer. Over the last three decades, his research has focused on the discovery and development of nucleic acid therapeutics, including antisense technology. He has published over 300 research papers and is listed as a co-inventor on more than 400 patents worldwide. He has edited four books on oligonucleotides and antisense technology, including “Advances in Nucleic Acid Therapeutics,” published in February 2019.

Dr. Agrawal received his Ph.D. in chemistry and conducted post-doctoral research at the MRC’s Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, U.K.

","source_id":1288},{"name":"Nancy Andrews, M.D., Ph.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Andrews is the former dean of the School of Medicine at Duke University, having served for 10 years in that role. Prior to her deanship, she was the G.R. Minot Professor and Dean for Basic Sciences and Graduate Studies at Harvard Medical School. Her research, funded by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the NIH, led to advances in understanding iron biology and iron diseases. She is an elected member of the National Academy of Sciences, the National Academy of Medicine and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Dr. Andrews also serves on the board of directors of the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and Novartis AG, and is a member of the MIT Corporation.

Dr. Andrews received her B.S. and M.S. from Yale University, her M.D. from Harvard Medical School and her Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Her clinical training was at Boston Children’s Hospital and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

","source_id":1289},{"name":"Louis Kunkel, Ph.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Kunkel is an internationally recognized geneticist who has devoted his career to understanding the molecular basis of, and developing novel therapies for, neuromuscular disorders. He is universally recognized for his 1986 identification of dystrophin as the causative gene in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. His current work centers on developing dystrophin independent therapies for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to complement existing therapies currently in development. A past Howard Hughes investigator and current member of the National Academy of Sciences, Dr. Kunkel has received numerous awards for his research, including the Welcome Trust Prize and the Gairdner Foundation International Award. He currently serves as a member of the Division of Genetics and Genomics at Boston Children’s Hospital, and as a professor of pediatrics and genetics at Harvard Medical School.

Dr. Kunkel received his B.A. from Gettysburg College and his Ph.D. from Johns Hopkins University.

","source_id":1290},{"name":"Francesco Muntoni, FRCPCH, FMedSci","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Muntoni’s research group led the development of the first genetic therapies in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and continues to drive cutting-edge exploration of the genetic roots of and investigational therapies for DMD and spinal muscular atrophy. Throughout his career, Dr. Muntoni has identified more than 30 neuromuscular disease genes and supported more than 30 clinical trials and natural history studies in pediatric neuromuscular diseases. He currently chairs the pediatric neurology department at University College London (UCL) and directs the Dubowitz Neuromuscular Centre, a leading research and clinical trial site for children affected by neuromuscular disorders. At Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, Dr. Muntoni serves as the theme lead for novel therapies at the Biomedical Research Centre.

Dr. Muntoni earned his M.D. from the Cagliari University Medical School in Italy. He completed a specialization in pediatric neurology and psychiatry at Sassari University Medical School in 1989. In addition to his role on Dyne’s Scientific Advisory Board, Dr. Muntoni serves as an advisor to Capricor Therapeutics, Sarepta Therapeutics and Pfizer.

","source_id":1291},{"name":"Jeffrey Statland, M.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Jeff Statland is an associate professor of neurology at the University of Kansas Medical Center and a leading researcher in the field of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD). He is the co-principal investigator for ReSolve (Clinical Trial Readiness to Solve Barriers to Drug Development in FSHD), an ongoing observational study that aims to validate new clinical outcome assessments and evaluate physiological biomarkers to support the design and implementation of future clinical trials. In addition to co-leading the ReSolve Natural History Study, Dr. Statland, with his collaborators at the University of Rochester Medical Center, is developing a disease-specific patient reported health inventory and molecular and neuroimaging biomarkers of disease activity for future FSHD clinical trials.

Dr. Statland holds a B.A. from Sarah Lawrence College, an M.F.A. from Emerson College and an M.D. from the University of Kansas School of Medicine. He completed residency training in the Department of Neurology at the University of Kansas Medical Center, and also conducted a fellowship in experimental therapeutics of neurologic disorders in the Department of Neurology at the University of Rochester Medical Center. He is board certified by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology.

","source_id":1299},{"name":"Charles Thornton, M.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"Dr. Thornton is the Saunders Distinguished Professor of Neuromuscular Research at the University of Rochester. He has been engaged in bench and clinical research on myotonic dystrophy for 30 years. Dr. Thornton received his B.S. from the University of Iowa and his M.D. from the University of Iowa’s Carver College of Medicine.","source_id":1300}]

He is chairman of the Board at Azafaros B.V., VectorY Therapeutics, and Numab Therapeutics AG. Previously Carlo served on the board of directors at EryDel SpA and Inversago Pharma. Carlo is also a founding member of the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium.

He received his medical degree from the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Italy.

","source_id":1930},{"name":"Vikram Karnani","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Vikram is president and chief executive officer of Collegium Pharmaceutical, a role he assumed in November 2024. Before joining Collegium, he served as executive vice president and president of global commercial operations and medical affairs (rare disease) at Amgen, where he led the integration and growth of the company’s rare disease business following its acquisition of Horizon Therapeutics. During nearly a decade at Horizon, Vikram held senior leadership roles, including president of global commercial operations and chief commercial officer. Earlier in his career, Vikram was vice president of the therapeutics and cell therapy business and held leadership roles in strategy and business development at Fresenius Kabi.

Vikram earned a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from the University of Mumbai, a master’s degree in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University, and an MBA from Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

","source_id":3304},{"name":"Dirk Kersten","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dirk is a general partner at Forbion, a leading European life science venture capital firm, where he focuses primarily on new investments. He is a physicist by training and previously was a partner at Gilde Healthcare Partners, where he led U.S. operations. Previously, Dirk was a managing director at INKEF Capital, where he was responsible for all healthcare investment activities. Dirk led a series of investments in Europe and the U.S. and is an active board member at a number of life science companies, including NorthSea Therapeutics B.V. and Synox Therapeutics Limited. Previously, Dirk served on the board of directors at Ascendis Pharma, Lanthio Pharma (acquired by Morphosys), Profibrix (acquired by The Medicines Company) and Nightbalance (acquired by Royal Philips).

Dirk received his M.S. in physics from the University of Groningen in the Netherlands.

","source_id":1284},{"name":"David Lubner","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

David Lubner is an accomplished financial leader in the life sciences space. He served as executive vice president and chief financial officer of Ra Pharma Inc., acquired by UCB in April 2020. Before joining Ra Pharma, David served as a member of the senior management team of Tetraphase Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and PharMetrics Inc., a leading patient-based pharmacy and medical claims data informatics company, which was acquired by IMS Health in 2005 and at ProScript, Inc., where Velcade® (bortezomib), a therapy widely used for treatment of the blood cancer multiple myeloma, was discovered. He serves as a member of the board of directors of Arcellx Inc., Vor Biopharma, Inc. and Cargo Therapeutics, Inc. and several other private companies. He previously served on the board of directors of Nightstar Therapeutics plc (acquired by Biogen), a company focused on the development of one-time retinal gene therapies for patients suffering from rare inherited retinal diseases, Therapeutics Acquisition Corporation and Gemini Therapeutics and Point Biopharma, Inc.

David is a Certified Public Accountant. He received his B.S. in business administration from Northeastern University and an M.S. in taxation from Bentley University.

","source_id":1286},{"name":"Brian Posner","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Brian has more than three decades of executive, investment and board leadership experience. He is the founder and president of Point Rider Group (UK) Ltd, an advisory and consulting firm that provides independent strategic counsel to senior executives, boards of directors and institutional investors. Previously, Brian served as president and CEO of ClearBridge Advisors, a $100 billion+ asset management firm, and as partner and managing director at Warburg Pincus, following senior investment roles at Hygrove Partners and Fidelity Investments. He has served on multiple boards, including his current role at Arch Capital Group (ACGL). He was previously chair of the AQR Funds and Bioverativ (BIVV) boards, and a director of Biogen (BIIB), Sotheby’s (BID) and The Mutual Fund Store.

Brian earned his B.A. from Northwestern University, where he is a Life Trustee and serves on the Advisory Board of its Center for the Study of Diversity and Democracy. He also received his M.B.A. from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.

","source_id":3237},{"name":"Catherine Stehman-Breen","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Catherine served as the chief executive officer and a member of the board of directors of Chroma Medicine, Inc. from December 2022 to December 2024. Previously, she was chief development officer at Obsidian Therapeutics and was an entrepreneur-in-residence with Atlas Venture. Before Atlas, she served as chief medical officer of Sarepta Therapeutics; vice president, clinical development at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals; and held senior leadership positions at Amgen, including as vice president, global development, where she led several therapeutic areas.

Catherine serves as a member of the board of directors of Generation Bio Co. and Tenaya Therapeutics, Inc. She earned her M.D. from the University of Chicago. She completed her residency and nephrology fellowship training at the University of Washington, where she also received an M.S. in epidemiology. Catherine served as a faculty member in the division of nephrology and remains an affiliate associate professor in the University of Washington School of Public Health, with more than 90 publications in medical journals.

[{"name":"Sudhir Agrawal, D.Phil.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Agrawal is a visiting professor in the Department of Medicine at the University of Massachusetts Medical School and a member of the advisory board of the Harvard Medical School Initiative for RNA Medicine. He is a founder and member of Arnay Sciences LLC. He is also a founder of Idera Pharmaceuticals, where he served in various leadership roles, including as chairman, CEO, president of research and chief scientific officer. Over the last three decades, his research has focused on the discovery and development of nucleic acid therapeutics, including antisense technology. He has published over 300 research papers and is listed as a co-inventor on more than 400 patents worldwide. He has edited four books on oligonucleotides and antisense technology, including “Advances in Nucleic Acid Therapeutics,” published in February 2019.

Dr. Agrawal received his Ph.D. in chemistry and conducted post-doctoral research at the MRC’s Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, U.K.

","source_id":1288},{"name":"Nancy Andrews, M.D., Ph.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Andrews is the former dean of the School of Medicine at Duke University, having served for 10 years in that role. Prior to her deanship, she was the G.R. Minot Professor and Dean for Basic Sciences and Graduate Studies at Harvard Medical School. Her research, funded by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the NIH, led to advances in understanding iron biology and iron diseases. She is an elected member of the National Academy of Sciences, the National Academy of Medicine and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Dr. Andrews also serves on the board of directors of the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and Novartis AG, and is a member of the MIT Corporation.

Dr. Andrews received her B.S. and M.S. from Yale University, her M.D. from Harvard Medical School and her Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Her clinical training was at Boston Children’s Hospital and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

","source_id":1289},{"name":"Louis Kunkel, Ph.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Kunkel is an internationally recognized geneticist who has devoted his career to understanding the molecular basis of, and developing novel therapies for, neuromuscular disorders. He is universally recognized for his 1986 identification of dystrophin as the causative gene in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. His current work centers on developing dystrophin independent therapies for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to complement existing therapies currently in development. A past Howard Hughes investigator and current member of the National Academy of Sciences, Dr. Kunkel has received numerous awards for his research, including the Welcome Trust Prize and the Gairdner Foundation International Award. He currently serves as a member of the Division of Genetics and Genomics at Boston Children’s Hospital, and as a professor of pediatrics and genetics at Harvard Medical School.

Dr. Kunkel received his B.A. from Gettysburg College and his Ph.D. from Johns Hopkins University.

","source_id":1290},{"name":"Francesco Muntoni, FRCPCH, FMedSci","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Muntoni’s research group led the development of the first genetic therapies in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and continues to drive cutting-edge exploration of the genetic roots of and investigational therapies for DMD and spinal muscular atrophy. Throughout his career, Dr. Muntoni has identified more than 30 neuromuscular disease genes and supported more than 30 clinical trials and natural history studies in pediatric neuromuscular diseases. He currently chairs the pediatric neurology department at University College London (UCL) and directs the Dubowitz Neuromuscular Centre, a leading research and clinical trial site for children affected by neuromuscular disorders. At Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children, Dr. Muntoni serves as the theme lead for novel therapies at the Biomedical Research Centre.

Dr. Muntoni earned his M.D. from the Cagliari University Medical School in Italy. He completed a specialization in pediatric neurology and psychiatry at Sassari University Medical School in 1989. In addition to his role on Dyne’s Scientific Advisory Board, Dr. Muntoni serves as an advisor to Capricor Therapeutics, Sarepta Therapeutics and Pfizer.

","source_id":1291},{"name":"Jeffrey Statland, M.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"

Dr. Jeff Statland is an associate professor of neurology at the University of Kansas Medical Center and a leading researcher in the field of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD). He is the co-principal investigator for ReSolve (Clinical Trial Readiness to Solve Barriers to Drug Development in FSHD), an ongoing observational study that aims to validate new clinical outcome assessments and evaluate physiological biomarkers to support the design and implementation of future clinical trials. In addition to co-leading the ReSolve Natural History Study, Dr. Statland, with his collaborators at the University of Rochester Medical Center, is developing a disease-specific patient reported health inventory and molecular and neuroimaging biomarkers of disease activity for future FSHD clinical trials.

Dr. Statland holds a B.A. from Sarah Lawrence College, an M.F.A. from Emerson College and an M.D. from the University of Kansas School of Medicine. He completed residency training in the Department of Neurology at the University of Kansas Medical Center, and also conducted a fellowship in experimental therapeutics of neurologic disorders in the Department of Neurology at the University of Rochester Medical Center. He is board certified by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology.

","source_id":1299},{"name":"Charles Thornton, M.D.","role":"","photo":"","bio":"Dr. Thornton is the Saunders Distinguished Professor of Neuromuscular Research at the University of Rochester. He directs the Muscular Dystrophy Cooperative Research Center in Rochester and the Myotonic Dystrophy Clinical Research Network, a multicenter consortium for clinical research and therapeutic trials. He has been engaged in bench and clinical research on myotonic dystrophy for 30 years. Dr. Thornton received his B.S. from the University of Iowa and his M.D. from the University of Iowa’s Carver College of Medicine.","source_id":1300}]
